positions.commentary: The speaker would not hold Nvidia because the leading-edge chip design sector is highly competitive and subject to significant technological disruption.
The speaker holds Texas Instruments because it manufactures analog chips with less risk of technological disruption compared to leading-edge designs.
The speaker notes that businesses like Airbnb offer less sophisticated technology compared to industrial gas businesses, but does not express a specific investment view on the company itself.

transcript:
Welcome to a new episode of the Best Anchors Talks podcast. Today, I have the pleasure of talking with Christian Billinger, chairman of Billinger for Vultening, AB, a privately held investment company based in Karlstad, Sweden. I decided to contact Christian after listening to him speak about quality investing, as I believe the investment style of Billinger for Vultening is pretty similar to that of best anchor stocks. We focus the conversation on quality investing and on the concept of hiding in plain sight. I hope you enjoy my conversation with Christian.
Yeah. So first of all, Christian, thanks for taking the time to be here.
I think the best place to start is by understanding your investment philosophy.
I know you're a quality investor, but how would you define quality investing in one sentence?
I'll give you maybe even two sentences if you want.
Thank you, Leandro. And thank you for inviting me onto the podcast. I'm excited to be here.
I listened to the first episode with Chris Mayer. You know, I'm a fan of his writing.
thought it was an excellent conversation. So thank you. I guess the core of quality investing
for me, Leandro, is this idea that stocks follow earnings. That's really the core of it. And I think usually
usually when you hear people defining quality investing, they will focus on the characteristics of the underlying
business and this idea of owning, so to speak, great businesses. So they'll refer to key metrics
like return on capital employed, organic growth, or aspects of the business model,
usually in the in the language of MOLs.
There are certainly things that I look at, but I think in a way, you know, you can take a different
perspective and look at it from the investor's point of view.
And if you take that perspective, the focus is really on owning businesses where the
returns that I can realize as an investor mainly, mainly come from the performance
of the underlying business. Obviously, plus minus a bit, depending on the price
or multiple we buy and sell at. But it's really about generating returns that reflect business performance.
And it follows from that that owning the best businesses should generate the highest
returns over long time periods, right? Because that's where you should see the highest
sustainable rate of earnings growth.
And one sort of advantage of defining quality investing in that way is that you also take valuation
into account. So it's not just about the business. Although it's mainly about the business quality.
it's also about not buying into that great business at a valuation
where you will almost inevitably not realize the sort of underlying performance.
You know, I think in another way, quality investing is simply investing, according to this
timeless principle, that you want to pay less than what you're receiving.
And it just happens that for us, the temperament, time rise, and risk management, the structure of how we operate, we end up in companies that are considered high quality quality.
But I think it's an important point, actually, that in some ways, quality investing is simply investing.
Yeah, I completely agree.
And I think the difficult thing about quality investing probably is that quality is somewhat subjective.
And despite me, I completely agree.
And despite many people claiming that there are many high-quality companies,
actually, the best quality investors claim to have investment universes of close to 50 companies.
I don't know if that's the same for you.
And if it is, what characteristics do the companies in your investment universe have in common?
So what are you looking for in a quality company?
Yes, in principle, we can look at any company in terms of market cap, geography,
industry, etc. But for us, the shortlist or universe, as you refer to Leandro,
it's also about 50 companies. You know, over time, that tends to expand a little bit, but call it 50.
And I think the question you're asking really relates to the how. You know, the previous question,
I think, covered the what, what is quality investing. And this is a question of how.
And the reason we end up with only, if you will, 50 companies
in there. Well, there's a few reasons. One of them is we need to, or we feel we need to be
able to understand these businesses. And so most companies actually fall away already at that stage
because we don't feel comfortable analyzing them. You know, it's the, it's the very well-known Buffett's,
the two hard pile that Buffett always refers to. So that's where most things end up for us as well.
The second reason there's so few companies in that investable universe is because we
need a, or we feel at least that there should be a pretty long track record, a paper record
of performance. And this relates to the idea of Lindy, right? And we also want that track record to be durable
or sustainable going forward so that we can actually assess the cash flows and thereby value the
business. So even more businesses fall away at that stage. And then thirdly, and maybe this is a more
general point, there's only so many great businesses out there. But by definition,
they can't all be great. Or certainly not much better than the average, right? And so, you know, while I agree that mean
reversion is probably a good assumption for most companies, there is clearly, clearly a small group of
companies that defy that investing sort of law of gravity. And, and, you know,
for us, what does that mean in practice? It means that we look at companies with sustainable
earnings growth. Usually they grow top line at, say, 5 to 10% organically.
They grow their earnings at least 8% to 12%. And over time, and this sort of goes back to the first
question, over time, we'd assume that we should realize a return of at least the 8 to 12%. In practice,
we end up in certain industries and types of business models. So, for instance,
we're, you know, highly exposed to industrials and consumer goods.
But that's not by sort of design.
That's just, that's a result of the bottom-up process we follow.
And, right, that's just the outcome of the philosophy we employ.
And there's certainly quality investors in technology and in consumer goods, in industrials, in financials, right?
So there's many different ways of doing this.
I think if you're looking for commonalities, there's probably more commonality when it comes
to the business model than when it comes to the industry.
So recurring revenues, flexible cost structures, low or no leverage, et cetera.
And I think they also tend to have an unusual or unique culture, which is difficult, sometimes, they're often difficult to put your finger on.
But, you know, if I look at our portfolio, we have things like MTU or MTAO engines or coloplast in there.
And they tend to be long term.
They're very focused on one or a few product segment.
their competitors and customers admire, openly admire what they do.
So, you know, there's, so that's perhaps less tangible.
But that's another example of why that list, you know, back to your question,
why is the list only 50 companies?
It's for a number of reasons, really.
And do you have a way of prioritizing this characteristics?
So, for example, is there something that you look in a business and you say,
okay, this is a must-have?
but maybe you look at another thing that you say, okay, maybe this company doesn't have this,
but that that's not like a requirement to be considered a high quality company?
I think for us, culture has got to be number one.
If it's not a business that is characterized by being long-term in their thinking,
that operates with great integrity, that, you know, where management is focused on shareholder value,
et cetera, then we can't invest in it.
So culture is certainly a must-have, as you refer to it.
And I think the idea that there needs to be something unique about the business is also a must-have, right?
So that could be a combination of culture, the product or service offering, the business model, the shareholder structure.
So culture and the uniqueness of the sort of mix of, you know, aspects of the business.
There must-haves.
I think for most other aspects of the business, it's a matter of trade-offs.
So, you know, one example, I like owning a business that has net cash on the balance sheet.
But in some industries, where we're invested, it's perfectly fine to operate with some gearing, right?
So if you're a consumer goods, you know, if you're a sort of staples company, you know,
I wouldn't expect you to be operating with net cash, you know.
We're happy with the moderator.
amount of gearing. And another example would be recurring revenues. You know, I'd like to see
recurring revenues, but in consumer goods, if we use that example again, generally, there's no contractually
recurring revenues. But, but in reality, the strength of brands and customer loyalty means that the
effect is similar. So I always think it's, it's important to focus on substance over form.
That's key when you're trying to sort of think from first principles.
Yeah, and regarding what you talked about, about the financial strength, I think many people tend to look at the balance sheet just to assess the financial position, but actually, in the cash flow statement, you also have a great source of financial strength.
So, so, for example, as you said, a company can have a net debt position, but maybe very stable and resilient cash flows.
So then actually its financial strength is very high.
I was, I was actually going to ask you, you, you know, what do you put more weight on, whether quantity
or qualitative characteristics? But I think you already answered this question, because if, if culture is
something you look at, then, I assume is qualitative.
And I wanted to know, like, qualitative characteristics are probably the most difficult
to analyze, which is, I think, maybe why there's an edge out there for certain investors.
If it was just numbers, then algorithms would rule investing. So I think they require quite a bit
of effort to understand. And also maybe some kind of humanistic interpretation, so to say,
that is probably absent in any quantitative variable. And my feeling is also that sometimes
it's impossible to understand these characteristics.
in depth unless you have followed the company for a long time, sometimes even years.
I mean, there are lots of investors that follow companies for several years before starting a position. So how
do you look for these characteristics and how do you analyze them? Are you one of those investors
that has to spend several years tracking our monitoring a position before
starting it? Or can you get more comfortable with qualitative characteristics in a shorter
period of time. Yeah, that's a great question.
And let me just first sort of go back to the first part of that, you know, where you talked about quantitative and
qualitative, qualitative. I guess in one important sense, to me, they're just two sides of the same coin.
I know, often, you know, we like to sort of separate the two as being
distinctly different ways of looking at a business. But to me, unless the qualitative
aspects translate into quantitative. It's pointless. So whether I think
something's a great business doesn't really matter unless that, you know, over time, that translates
into sustainably high earnings growth. But you're absolutely right, of course, that in terms
of the analysis, we're much more focused on the qualitative, right? And I think that's, for me,
that's saying, that's the same thing as saying it's process over outcome. And we're looking at the
underlying drivers as opposed to reported financials in the in the short to medium
term, right? Because the reported financials can have a large element of noise in there. So,
for, for instance, if I think back to the years leading up to the great financial crisis in sort of
207, 209, if you looked at house builders or miners in 2007, you know, and you looked at the, and you
look at the sort of, if you only looked at the numbers they reported, you only looked at the numbers
they reported, you would assume they were terrific, incredible, wonderful,
durable earnings streams, right? Or if you looked at some of the so-called pandemic winners in 2020,
you know, whether it's a Peloton or a Zoom or whatever, you could be tempted into thinking their companies
with sustainably high earnings growth. But obviously, that's, I don't think that's
the way to sort of go about it if you want to own great businesses for the for the long term.
And so, so just to address that part of your question, I think valuation matters, right? But the
forward PE matters much less for us and many other quality investors because we're focused on the long,
longer term, right? The long term time arise. And most of your returns, if you're a long-term
investor in great businesses at least will come from the underlying business.
So what I do want to avoid is buying at levels where it's obvious or almost obvious that we won't
fully participate in the value creation, right? So even if you're seeing 10 or 12 or 15% earnings growth
and you're buying it 40 times and that reverts to say 25 times, you know, you're not getting 10 or 12
15%. You're getting something much less than that. I would say reality, they tend to go hand in hand.
And so if you rightly identify a business that continues to outperform operationally, they don't tend to see much multiple contraction, right?
So it's it's still better to look at the business and the qualitative aspects.
And the other reasons for that are, number one, if it's a great business, the intrinsic value should increase over time.
And two, the valuation part of it is just such an inexact.
science. We try not to worry about it too much in detail, at least, right? So we take, you know,
we obviously try to build some sort of model and valuation to understand the drivers, but we're not
looking at the decimal points. I'm sorry for that long sort of, long way of addressing the first part of your
question there, Leandro. I should also say in the, just to address the second part of it.
You know, there's a few reasons, I think, that these qualitative aspects are maybe often less looked at.
And as you said, often I think, they require you to look at a business for much longer, right?
So you can easily easily pull out the financials in an hour or two and sort of look at the earnings track record and margin progression.
And quality takes longer to understand.
and appreciate fully, I think. And one reason, in my view, at least, is that
there's this institutional constraint. So I used to work, you know, for a few different fund management
companies. And if you're an analyst at an asset manager, you can't just pitch an idea to the PM and say,
this is a great business, right? They want something more specific and they usually
want to trigger because they have to deliver performance in the next three or six or 12
months or sometimes even on a monthly basis.
And so they're, so they're not just going to sort of buy something because I think it's a great business.
The qualitative aspects of a business, though, as I say, sort of alluded to, I, you know, I think are the
ones that drive the sustainably high earnings growth.
Some are more obvious.
So if you look at the business model, for instance, and this is coming back to your second,
the second part of your question, Leandro,
that, you know, business model, I think you can figure out more quickly, so you can maybe have
a checklist that looks at recurring revenues or the cost structure or the balance sheet. But I think
when it comes to things like culture, it takes longer to fully understand and appreciate a business. And
often you need to sort of, you know, meet with the company or speak to former employees or sort of pick up
stories and observe what goes on.
So, you know, I'll give you an example of a holding of ours, which is Markell.
And I went to visit Tom Gaynor in Richmond, Virginia, about a year ago.
And I spent an afternoon with him, we had lunch.
We went to his office and, you know, just sort of observing the way he interacted with other people
and the way he is suggested to me, at least, that he's someone that I can rely on to be a steward
of my, my or our capital.
And having said that, I know there's something.
also a tendency in some so-called value investing circles to say that if you're frugal,
that means you have integrity and your shareholder value focused. I don't necessarily agree with that,
you know, we're, I know it probably comes, it goes back to Buffett, but if I look at LVMA,
which is another one of our large holdings, there's nothing that is ordinary about Bernard Ornard's
lifestyle, but I still think he's an outstanding steward of capital. So it's once again,
And once again, sorry, it's substance over form, really.
But that's sort of how I look at it, you know, when it comes to how quickly can you pick up on these different
aspects of a business.
So I guess the answer to your question is quicker in some aspects and certainly more slowly in some others.
Well, I guess in the case of LVMH, maybe if Bernard was frugal, that would be even, like, worse.
That would be terrified.
Yeah.
So staying a bit on.
this topic. I want to speak a bit about management now that we had Tom Gainer and Bernard Arnold
come up. What role does management play in your search for a high quality business?
Because we have seen, for example, investors such as Peter Lynch claiming that you, like, it's best to
invest in a business that can be run by, quote unquote, an idiot. Because probably sometime that
will happen. Like, managers are not forever. Probably, I think, cultures are
forever. But obviously, a bad management team can erode a culture. So what way do you put on
on management and on management continuity? Yeah, great, great question. I think, in most cases,
to us, the business is more, to the extent you can separate the two, the business is more important
than the management team. But we, but it's similar to us, it's similar to the business. It's similar
to the way we look at valuations, we certainly want to avoid investing with lousy or bad
management, right? Because I've seen too many great businesses or great assets underperforming because
of poor execution. And so, you know, a couple of examples of large, well-known companies that we've been
invested in where we feel that that's been an issue. Unilever is one of them. You know, I can, I think it's
plain to see for most people the extraordinary sort of assets they have in terms of the brand.
and the distribution network and the emerging markets reach and everything.
But execution has not been impressive at all. I mean, it's, it's been very disappointing, actually.
And obviously, there's management change happening there now. And I don't know, to what extent it's
it's Alan Jope's sort of fault and to what extent it's Paul Paul Paulman, who was before him.
But so that's one example where we feel that, you know, potentially great business.
but if there's any doubt, we sort of, ultimately, I get to a point where I ask myself,
okay, capital preservation is my priority number one.
So if I feel uncomfortable or I'm unsure about this, you know, move on, just sort of, you know, try
and exit and move on because there's so many other opportunities, including our other current
holding or existing holdings.
Another example would be the testing inspection certification companies.
We've been invested in Intertech and SGS for a number of years.
But we feel that once again, like Unleaver, they're potentially great businesses.
And in the past, they've delivered tremendous shareholder returns.
But partly because of shareholders, etc., they've been underinvesting for a number of years.
And smaller, more nimble competitors have been taking share and partly at the expense
of these large players, and so therefore we've sold out of them.
So I think in cases, Leandro, where we see what we feel feel is sort of obviously poor execution,
that would be an issue.
If you look at the upside, on the other hand, yes, exceptional performance will often largely be driven
driven by exceptional people and exceptional management.
So, you know, in our portfolio, Berkshire and LVMH would be two obvious examples.
I mean, they're so obvious.
they're probably not great examples.

intimate care business.

And another example would be Diageo, where I feel Ivan Menezzes,

Yep.
And in this management.
analysis that you do. How important is alignment and compensation? So I feel that

than 100 years old. So it's actually quite difficult to find a manager if it's not

often used word alignment, right? So in principle, I'm all for financial incentives
to management and alignment, but I feel that if you can pick businesses where there's, you know,

so that they could incentivize him because his stake was already like in the billions.

I agree with you.

they're not, they're not led by the founders and, and, and, you know, management does not have a significant

Okay, so now that we have discussed quality investing in general, I mean, we have still some discussion to do, but I want to shift gears a little bit and talk about the concept of hiding in plain sight.

because if they were obviously fairly valued, then you would have enjoyed market returns.
So why do you think high quality companies fly under the radar so much?
I mean, like, many compounders are obvious, like, you can look back at the chart.
The past is, everyone can look at the past, but few of these companies actually end up making it into many
portfolios. I see this is especially true in the portfolios of professional investors.
So what do you think people choose to, quote, unquote, ignore these companies, rather than building a portfolio
of companies that have already demonstrated that they are high-quality companies?
I agree with you once again. I think often these businesses are, are, so to speak,
hiding in plain sight. I think there's a few reasons. So, number one,
Institutional investors often have compressed time horizons.
And so if you're looking at something on a, say, six to 12 or even 18-month horizon,
multiple expansion or contraction will play an outsized role for returns as, you know,
as opposed to earnings, the earnings trajectory.
And, you know, most great businesses trade at a meaningful premium to the earnings trajectory.
And, you know, most great businesses trade at a meaningful premium to the market. And, and therefore, you know,

and, therefore, I'm going to look elsewhere.

reversion is inevitable and will affect all companies over five or 10 years or whatever.
You know, for most companies, that is true.

And I think we can come back to this idea.
But I think if you look at certainly the sell side, and I think often the buy side,
most people have gone through that kind of training and they therefore assume that mean
reversion will affect all companies they look at.

I think often these so-called quality businesses are in pretty boring industries.

So they're not.
They're not headline stuff, really.

roads.

EPS growth might be 8 to 12 or 8 to 14 or something.
You know, clearly they're not slow-growing businesses, but they're not super-fast
